and Arora et al. (2018) for noise robustness). The lottery ticket hypothesis offers a complementary
perspective on this relationship—that larger networks might explicitly contain simpler representations.

We introduce a novel framework for the estima-
tion of the posterior distribution over the weights
of a neural network, based on a new probabilistic
interpretation of adaptive optimisation algorithms
such as ADAGRAD and ADAM.
We demon-
strate the effectiveness of our Bayesian ADAM
method, BADAM, by experimentally showing that
the learnt uncertainties correctly relate to the
weights’ predictive capabilities by weight pruning.
We also demonstrate the quality of the derived un-
certainty measures by comparing the performance
of BADAM to standard methods in a Thompson
sampling setting for multi-armed bandits, where
good uncertainty measures are required for an
agent to balance exploration and exploitation.

In practice, neural networks tend to be dramatically overparameterized. Distillation (Ba & Caruana,
2014; Hinton et al., 2015) and pruning (LeCun et al., 1990; Han et al., 2015) rely on the fact that
parameters can be reduced while preserving accuracy. Even with sufﬁcient capacity to memorize
training data, networks naturally learn simpler functions (Zhang et al., 2016; Neyshabur et al., 2014;
Arpit et al., 2017). Contemporary experience (Bengio et al., 2006; Hinton et al., 2015; Zhang et al.,
2016) and Figure 1 suggest that overparameterized networks are easier to train. We show that dense
networks contain sparse subnetworks capable of learning on their own starting from their original
initializations. Several other research directions aim to train small or sparse networks.

## Neural network pruning

Across the ~100-paper corpus, one document carries essentially all the substantive content on this topic: **`1803.03635.pdf` — "The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis: Finding Sparse, Trainable Neural Networks"** (Frankle & Carbin, ICLR 2019). The other hits (EfficientNet `1905.11946`, SGDR `1608.03983`, Bayesian NNs `1811.03679`, FlashAttention `2205.14135`) only mention pruning in passing — in reference lists or a one-line experiment — so the answer below is built from `1803.03635.pdf`, with those secondary mentions noted at the end.

### What pruning is and why it matters
Pruning is the family of techniques for **eliminating unnecessary weights from a trained neural network**. It can reduce parameter counts by **more than 90% without harming accuracy**, which shrinks storage/model size and lowers the energy and compute cost of inference (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 1, abstract and Introduction). The lineage cited runs from LeCun et al. 1990 and Hassibi & Stork 1993 (Optimal Brain Surgeon) through Han et al. 2015 and Li et al. 2016 (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 1; the Hassibi & Stork "Optimal Brain Surgeon" reference is on p. 11).

### The central tension the paper addresses
Although a pruned network is small, you generally **cannot just train that small architecture from scratch** — the sparse architectures produced by pruning are harder to train from the start and reach lower accuracy than the original dense network. Figure 1 demonstrates this: randomly-sampled sparse subnetworks learn slower and top out at lower test accuracy the sparser they get (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 1–2). This is why pruning has historically been an *inference-time* efficiency tool rather than a *training-time* one.

### The Lottery Ticket Hypothesis
The paper's contribution is that a **standard magnitude-pruning technique uncovers sparse subnetworks ("winning tickets") that CAN be trained effectively in isolation** — if you keep their original initialization. Formally: a randomly-initialized dense network contains a subnetwork (mask `m` over parameters `θ₀`) that, trained alone from `m⊙θ₀`, matches the full network's test accuracy in at most the same number of iterations, with `‖m‖₀ ≪ |θ|` (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 2).

### The pruning algorithm (how a winning ticket is found)
The central experiment (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 2):
1. Randomly initialize the network `f(x; θ₀)`.
2. Train for `j` iterations to `θⱼ`.
3. **Prune `p%` of the smallest-magnitude weights** in `θⱼ`, creating mask `m`.
4. **Reset** the surviving weights to their *original* `θ₀` values — yielding the winning ticket `f(x; m⊙θ₀)`.

The key novelty vs. prior work is step 4: instead of keeping trained weights or re-initializing, each surviving connection is reset to its value from *before* training. They use **unstructured, layer-wise magnitude pruning** (remove the lowest-magnitude weights per layer; output-connection weights pruned at half rate), as in Han et al. 2015 (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 3).

**One-shot vs. iterative:** one-shot prunes once; the paper mainly uses **iterative pruning**, repeating train→prune→reset over `n` rounds, removing `p^(1/n)%` of surviving weights per round. Iterative pruning finds winning tickets at smaller sizes than one-shot (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 2). The cost is that each iterative experiment trains the network 15–30 times consecutively, which is why they use an abbreviated training schedule (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 40).

### Key empirical findings
- Winning tickets are consistently **10–20% (or less) of the original size** for MNIST/CIFAR10 fully-connected and convolutional architectures (Lenet, Conv-2/4/6, Resnet-18, VGG-19; see architecture table, `1803.03635.pdf`, p. 3).
- Above that size threshold, winning tickets **learn faster AND reach higher test accuracy** than the original network. On Lenet, early-stopping occurs ~38% earlier at `Pm≈21%`, and test accuracy peaks (+0.3 pts) around `Pm≈13.5%` before declining; performance regresses to baseline by `Pm≈3.6%` (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 4).
- **Initialization is essential.** If you keep the pruned *structure* (mask `m`) but randomly re-initialize, the subnetwork learns progressively slower and loses accuracy after little pruning — e.g., at `Pm=21%` the winning ticket reaches minimum validation loss **2.51× faster** and is ~0.5 pts more accurate than the reinitialized version (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 4). Structure alone does not explain the success (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 3).
- **Better generalization:** at iteration 50,000 winning tickets show up to +0.35 pts test accuracy even though nearly all networks hit 100% training accuracy, i.e. a smaller train/test gap. The paper frames this as an "Occam's Hill" — accuracy rises then falls as you prune, with overparameterized and over-pruned models both suboptimal (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 4 and p. 9).
- **Caveat for deeper nets:** finding winning tickets via this magnitude-pruning strategy is sensitive to learning rate and requires learning-rate *warmup* at higher rates (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 2).

### Why it matters conceptually
Pruning is tied to the observation that neural networks are **dramatically overparameterized**; both distillation and pruning rely on the fact that parameters can be reduced while preserving accuracy (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 10, related work). The lottery-ticket view reframes this: a large network is valuable partly because it contains many candidate sparse subnetworks, one of which SGD can recover — suggesting future training schemes that prune early, and design of better sparse architectures/initializations (`1803.03635.pdf`, p. 3, Implications).

### Secondary mentions in the corpus (context only, not substance)
- **`1905.11946.pdf` (EfficientNet)**, p. 9 — cites Han et al.'s "Deep Compression" (pruning + quantization + Huffman coding) as related model-compression work.
- **`1608.03983.pdf` (SGDR)**, p. 11 — same Deep Compression reference in its bibliography.
- **`1811.03679.pdf` (Practical Bayesian Neural Networks / BADAM)**, p. 1 and p. 8 — uses **weight pruning** as a downstream test: it ranks weights by signal-to-noise ratio `|µ|/σ` to show learned uncertainties correspond to weights' predictive importance. This is pruning-as-evaluation, not a pruning method per se.

**Bottom line:** In this corpus, "neural network pruning" is authoritatively covered by the Lottery Ticket Hypothesis paper (`1803.03635.pdf`): pruning removes >90% of weights without hurting accuracy, and its central result is that magnitude-pruning + rewinding to original initialization uncovers small, trainable "winning ticket" subnetworks (10–20% of original size) that train as fast or faster and generalize slightly better than the full network — with the initialization, not just the sparse structure, being the crucial ingredient.
